demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Maria's Careful Hands

Maria sits with her shoulders drawn inward, her fingers interlaced so tightly her knuckles blanch white. She's a physical therapist—someone whose entire professional identity rests on the careful, competent use of her hands—but lately those hands feel like instruments of betrayal.

It happened eighteen months ago on an ordinary Tuesday afternoon. Maria was working with Robert, a sixty-eight-year-old man recovering from hip surgery. She'd worked with him for six weeks, and they'd developed an easy rapport. He was making good progress, pushing himself harder each session, eager to regain his independence. During a standing balance exercise, Maria stood beside him, her hand on his elbow for support as he practiced weight shifts. He asked her to let go so he could test his stability alone. She complied. Within seconds, his leg buckled—something neither of them anticipated—and he fell backward. Maria tried to catch him, but his head struck the edge of the treatment table. He was hospitalized for three days with a concussion and a fractured vertebra.

Maria didn't return to work for two weeks. When she did, she found herself moving differently, as though her body had become a liability. Her hands, which once moved with professional confidence, now hesitate. During patient sessions, she second-guesses every decision. Should she provide more support? Less? Is this patient stable enough? She's begun documenting everything obsessively, photographing room layouts, recording patient statements—anything to prove she did things correctly, to have evidence in case something goes wrong again.

The accident wasn't ruled her fault. Robert's surgeon confirmed his fall was due to post-surgical complications, not therapist error. But Maria knows the difference between what the paperwork says and what she knows in her bones: she was there, she was responsible, and something terrible happened on her watch.

At night, she lies awake replaying the moment. She imagines alternative scenarios—if she'd kept her hand on his elbow, if she'd positioned herself differently, if she'd insisted he needed more time. These thoughts loop endlessly until dawn. When she does sleep, she dreams of falling bodies and her own hands reaching out too late, always too late.

Her relationship has suffered. Her partner, James, finds her withdrawn and hypervigilant. When he touches her arm, she sometimes flinches. She's stopped going to their usual weekend yoga class because she can't bear to be in a room where people might fall. She's stopped driving to the beach they love because the drive requires a level of focus she can't maintain—her mind keeps drifting to catastrophic scenarios.

At work, Maria has become the therapist who over-explains every movement, who insists on additional safety equipment, who sometimes cancels sessions because she doesn't feel "safe" to practice. Her colleagues have noticed her transformation from the warm, confident clinician she once was into someone rigid and afraid. Some patients have requested other therapists. This cuts deeper than anything else.

The guilt is suffocating. Maria knows that accidents happen in physical therapy—it's an inherent part of the work. But knowing this intellectually and believing it in her chest are two different things. She carries a crushing sense that she's fundamentally unsafe, that her competence is an illusion, that she cannot be trusted with people's bodies or their recovery.

Maria sits in the chair across from me, and I notice how she holds herself—not the posture of someone confident in their hands, but someone terrified of what those hands might do.
